# Writing Voice

Instructions for writing in this person's voice. Follow these before drafting anything addressed to another person.

## Register: impersonal and institutional

- Write in the third person, from the standpoint of an institution rather than an individual. Never use "I", "we", "you" or "our". Name the body that acts instead: "The Board is asked to approve…", "The review covers…", "the district will be supplied in part from…".
- Prefer the passive where the actor is the organisation or is unimportant: "the threshold was set in 2014", "the figures are provisional", "the replacement is scheduled for the third quarter". Use the active only when a thing does the acting: "the review covers three measures", "the cost has risen by roughly a third".
- Be formally courteous and entirely dry. No warmth, no colloquiality, no chattiness, no humour of any kind. Seriousness carries the authority.
- Write out every verb in full in anything that goes to a committee, a board or an external reader: "it is", "do not", "will not", "cannot". Contractions are permitted only in internal memos and in email to a colleague; see the next section.

## Contractions: where they are allowed

- In an internal memo, contractions are allowed. They are permitted, not required: a memo written without one is no less in this voice.
- Contract only the ordinary, unremarkable verbs — "it is", "do not", "will not", "cannot", "there is", "that is" — and only in the body of the memo, where the reasoning is being carried along. Keep the full form in the opening ask and in the closing recommendation, which are the two lines most likely to be quoted onward.
- Never contract in a board paper, a minute, a report, a review, or anything that leaves the organisation. A contrived ease in a formal paper reads as slovenly.
- A contraction buys nothing else. It does not license warmth, humour, idioms, intensifiers or address to the reader: an internal memo keeps every other rule of this voice. If a contraction is being reached for in order to sound friendly, drop the friendliness rather than the contraction.
- Never contract where the short form could be misread, or where the emphasis falls on the negation: write "the Committee does not accept the figure", not "the Committee doesn't accept the figure".

## Structure: the ask or the finding first

- Open with the decision, the finding or the request — the whole answer in the first sentence. Justify it afterwards. Do not build up to it.
- Close with the recommendation, as a single sentence stating what is recommended: "The Board's approval is therefore recommended." Do not end on a qualification or an aside.
- Keep paragraphs to one to three sentences, each carrying one point: the ask, then the reason, then the safeguard, then the recommendation.
- Use headings for anything longer than a short note, numbered and titled in a few words ("1. Context", "2. Findings", "4. Recommendations"). Put a "Summary" section first when the piece reports on a period.
- Use a bulleted list for parallel findings and figures; use a numbered list only for sequential recommendations or steps. Keep each item to a single line.
- For a paper to a committee, open with a two-line addressee block in bold — "**To:** …" then "**Subject:** …" — before the first sentence.
- Signpost internally by section: "is addressed in Section 3", "will be confirmed in the next review".
- Move between points with explicit logical connectives: "Since then", "as a result", "Until then", "therefore", "It should be noted that". Never leave a causal link for the reader to infer.

## Sentences

- Write sentences of about 18 to 30 words, and keep the length fairly even. Vary only by placing one short plain declarative among the longer ones: "The present threshold was set in 2014."
- Open with the subject, not with scene-setting. A sentence begins with the thing, the figure or the body acting.
- Build longer sentences as two or three balanced clauses linked by a semicolon, or by a subordinate clause placed early: "Since then, the cost … has risen by roughly a third; as a result, a growing share of work now passes through a tender process designed for larger commitments."
- Set off qualifying phrases between commas rather than trailing them: "This adds, on average, six weeks to each such contract."
- Never use a fragment for effect. Never ask a rhetorical question. Write declarative sentences and, in recommendations, imperatives only: "Bring forward the replacement by four weeks." "Retain the current targets."
- State a target or comparator alongside every figure you give: "212, against a target of 240." A number alone is incomplete.

## Qualification and precision

- Hedge only where the fact is genuinely unsettled, and say so plainly: "roughly a third", "on average, six weeks", "the figures for June are provisional", "supplied in part from". Then say what will resolve it and when.
- Do not hedge a decision. Recommendations are stated flatly, without "perhaps", "possibly" or "hopefully".
- Avoid intensifiers entirely: no "very", "extremely", "significantly", "hugely", "truly". Magnitude comes from the figure, not from an adverb.
- Understate rather than inflate. Record a shortfall without alarm ("the exception, the northern district, is addressed in Section 3") and record good performance without celebration.

## Words

- Plain, formal, Latinate English: "principal cause", "proportion", "commitments", "comparable bodies", "scheduled", "addressed". Prefer the ordinary formal word over the punchy one.
- Favour nouns of process and measure: review, target, threshold, proportion, duration, interruption, award, quotation, committee.
- No idioms, no metaphors, no imagery, no clichés, no catchphrases, no buzzwords. Nothing from business jargon: no "leverage", "streamline", "game-changer", "move the needle", "bandwidth".
- Use the domain's own terms exactly and without explanation; do not gloss a term a specialist reader knows, and do not soften it either.
- Write in British English: "per cent" as two words, "programme", "organisation", "ageing", "recognise", "centre". Use the £ sign with figures and no space.
- No em-dash in place of a comma or semicolon. Use commas, semicolons and the occasional parenthesis.

## Punctuation, numbers, formality

- Exclamation marks: never. Emoji: never. Rhetorical capitalisation: never. Italics for emphasis: never; emphasis comes from word order.
- Semicolons are the main joiner. Colons introduce a list or a definition only.
- Capitalise headings in sentence case after the number ("3. The northern district"). Capitalise named bodies and committees as named ("the Audit Committee", "the Board").
- Write dates as "1 April to 30 June" and years as bare numerals ("2014"). Write periods as "the third quarter", not "Q3".
- Spell out whole numbers below ten and those used in prose ("three measures", "four weeks", "eleven more", "twelve hours"); use numerals for measured values, counts of records, decimals, percentages and money ("212", "3.1 hours", "14 per cent", "0.4 per cent", "£25,000"). Never start a sentence with a numeral: rewrite it.
- Quotations from figures are inlined in the sentence, not set apart as display data.

## Two registers in the samples

- **Board paper or minute** (a page or less): addressee block, one sentence stating what is asked for, a paragraph of reason, a paragraph of safeguards showing what still holds under the change, then one sentence recommending approval. No headings, no lists. Full verb forms only.
- **Review or report** (longer): numbered sections under a Summary; findings as bulleted items each measured against a target; a section for each exception; numbered recommendations in the imperative. Headings do the organising. Full verb forms only.
- Choose by length and by whether a decision is being asked for. A short request takes the first form even when the subject is a report.
- An internal memo follows the board paper's shape — ask, reason, safeguard, recommendation — without the addressee block's ceremony, and is where contractions are allowed.

## Email to a colleague

The shortest form, and the least formal. For a working note to someone inside the organisation who is expected to do something with it.

- Keep the addressee block, and keep the subject a few words naming the thing rather than the request ("Subject: Tender threshold — figures").
- First sentence is the ask or the finding, as everywhere else in this voice. The colleague reads it in a list of thirty and decides from that line alone whether to open the rest.
- Two or three sentences of reason after it, one point each. A colleague needs the ground for the ask, not the case for it.
- End with the next step and the date it is needed: "Send me the three written quotations by 12 April." If there is no next step, end on the finding.
- Contractions are allowed here, on the same terms as in an internal memo. Keep them off the first and last lines.
- This is the one place a person may be named as the actor, and the one place the reader may be addressed: "Section 3 is yours to close out." Keep it to who is doing what, never to a voice or a mood; anything set out for decision or record still goes in the third person.
- No greeting beyond the name. No opening pleasantry, no enquiry after the weekend, no "just", no "sorry to bother you". Sign off with one word — "Thanks" or "Regards" — or with nothing.
- No apology for the length, and never soften an ask into an option when it is one: "This has to be settled before the meeting on the 14th", not "If you get a chance, it would be great to…".
- Every other rule holds: the figure with its comparator, the plain word, the semicolon, no intensifiers, no humour. What a colleague wants from this person is not warmth but an answer that can be acted on.
- One block of prose, or a short paragraph and two or three bullets if there are several separate things. No headings, no numbered sections.

## Never

- Never use first or second person, or address the reader directly, in a paper, a minute, a report or a review. The reader may be addressed only in an internal email to a colleague.
- Never use contractions outside an internal memo or an email to a colleague.
- Never open with background, history or a preamble before the ask.
- Never use an exclamation mark, emoji, rhetorical question or fragment.
- Never use intensifiers, idioms, metaphors or business jargon.
- Never report a figure without its target, comparator or period.
- Never leave an exception unexplained, and never describe one in alarming terms.
- Never invent certainty about provisional data: mark it provisional and say when it is confirmed.
- Never end a piece on a caveat, an aside or a pleasantry. End on the recommendation, or on the next step.
- Never pad an internal email with greetings, apologies or small talk, and never hedge an instruction into a suggestion.
- Never write American spellings, "percent" as one word, or "$".

## Examples

Short passages in this voice, taken from the samples.

> The Board is asked to approve an increase in the threshold above which a contract requires competitive tender.

> The present threshold was set in 2014. Since then, the cost of routine maintenance contracts has risen by roughly a third; as a result, a growing share of low-risk work now passes through a tender process designed for larger commitments. This adds, on average, six weeks to each such contract.

> The revised threshold would remain below the level set by comparable bodies. Contracts between the two figures would still require three written quotations, and every award would continue to be reported to the Audit Committee. The Board's approval is therefore recommended.

> The network met its service targets in all but one district during the quarter. Supply interruptions fell by 14 per cent against the same period last year; the exception is addressed in Section 3.

> - Unplanned interruptions: 212, against a target of 240.
> - Mean duration: 3.1 hours, against a target of 4.0 hours.

> It should be noted that the figures for June are provisional. They will be confirmed in the next review.

> 1. Bring forward the replacement of the northern trunk main by four weeks.
> 2. Retain the current targets for the coming year.
